summary:
Tver Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, and the national framework is where the operative risk for a transgender visitor sits. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) is the assessment standard used here; it contains no information specific to Tver Oblast beyond that national framework, so this record reports the national position as it applies to the oblast.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage is prohibited and legal gender transition is banned. The law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed in 2023, which effectively banned trans-specific healthcare and ended legal gender recognition. The Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that, explicitly, "justifies" gender transition.

Foreigners who breach these statutes face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and national government travel warnings state this directly to LGBT travellers. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings addressed to LGBT travellers.

Enforcement since the extremist designation has been sustained. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the International LGBT Movement or for displaying its symbols since November 2023, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. The same reporting records 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, most of them on social media. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, and "gay propaganda" fines for individuals reach 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) alongside detention of up to 15 days.

Physical coercion accompanies the legal exposure. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed. A Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility in December 2024. A transgender woman was held for nine months at a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in 2021 and forced to take testosterone before escaping.

The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume has grown alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024, when at least three LGBTQ-friendly Moscow venues were raided on the same night. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation.

The UK Home Office note is a document about Russia as a whole and is used as the assessment framework here; its absence of oblast-level findings is itself relevant to how much local variance a visitor should expect to find in Tver Oblast. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tver Oblast live under the same statutes as visitors on the core questions, with the additional exposure of having no exit as a mitigation. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement nationwide, and administrative liability under article 20.3 has produced 81 convictions across 98 cases since January 2024, most concerning LGBT symbols posted on social media.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are unavailable to residents: the 2023 law bars gender reassignment surgery and changes to legal gender on official documents, so documents cannot be corrected to match a resident's lived gender. Same-sex marriage is unavailable as well, and consensual same-sex activity is not itself criminalised.

Propaganda fines for individuals reach 400,000 rubles (about £3,600), with detention of up to 15 days available as an alternative, and extremism charges carry penalties of up to 12 years in prison.

UK asylum assessment treats LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as members of a particular social group under the refugee convention.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tver Oblast-specific enforcement data, incident reporting, local police practice or regional facility information appears in the source inventory. The UK Home Office note states expressly that it contains no information specific to this division beyond the national framework, so oblast-level variation in how the national statutes are applied is unresolved rather than established as absent.

The inventory does not resolve how the oblast's own administrative codes or regional public-order provisions interact with the federal extremism and propaganda statutes, and no Tver-specific court outcomes are sourced. Whether any local LGBTQ+ venues, support services or safe spaces operate in Tver Oblast is not sourced either.

Figures from Human Rights Watch are national counts as at 30 June 2025 and are not broken down by region; attributing any share of them to Tver Oblast would be unsupported.
